IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
CIVIL APPEAL NO. ______ OF 2026
[DIARY NO(S). 52885 OF 2024]
SATYENDRA GAUTAM                             Appellant (s)
                                VERSUS
THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH & ORS.           Respondent(s)
O R D E R 
1. Delay condoned.
2. Leave granted.
3. This appeal is filed against the order dated
02.11.2023 passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh
at Jabalpur in W.P.No. 22223 of 2023.
4. Brief facts leading to filing of the civil appeal
are that the appellant applied for the post of Gram
Rojgar Sahayak in the year 2015.  On the basis of the
said application, Zila Panchayat authorities issued a
final list, in which the appellant was given 114.80
marks and placed him at Serial No. 6.  However, such
order of appointment was not given to the appellant.
5. The appellant approached the High Court by filing
a writ petition, which was disposed of by order dated
24.11.2020, directing that the appellant may approach
the Zila Panchayat seeking redressal of his grievance.

--- Page 158 ---
2
6. In view of the directions issued by the High
Court, the appellant approached the Chief Executive
Officer, Zila Panchayat.  Subsequently, it is on the
basis of the appellant’s representation/appeal that
the Commissioner, Sagar, Madhya Pradesh, issued the
order dated 01.08.2023 directing that the appellant
may be appointed.  Pursuant to the directions of the
Commissioner,  the  appellant  was  appointed  on
25.09.2023.
7. We have heard Mr. Varun Thakur, learned counsel
appearing for the appellant and Ms. Mrinal Gopal
Elker, learned counsel appearing for the respondent –
State and also Mr. Akshat Srivastava, learned counsel
appearing for Respondent No. 5.      
8. Mr. Varun Thakur, learned counsel appearing for
the appellant, submits that the appellant worked from
05.09.2023 to 05.12.2025 and working from 29.01.2025
till today. The respondent no. 5 filed a writ petition
challenging the power of the Commissioner in directing
appointment of the appellant. It is pertinent to note
that  the  appointment  of  the  appellant  was  not
challenged on merits. The High Court by an order
impugned in this appeal set aside the appointment of
the appellant on the ground that the Commissioner did

--- Page 159 ---
3
not have the power to direct appointment.
9. Though Mr. Akshat Srivastava, learned counsel
appearing for Respondent No. 5, has strongly opposed
the civil appeal and supported the reasoning given by
the High Court, but in the facts and circumstances of
the case, we see no justification for the High Court
to interfere with the order of appointment passed in
favour of the appellant.
10. It  is  submitted  by  Ms.  Mrinal  Gopal  Elker,
learned counsel appearing on behalf of the State that
the scope of power of the Commissioner needs to be
examined.  
11. Having considered the matter in detail, we are of
the opinion that the appellant has been working in the
post from September, 2023 and there is no doubt about
the fact that the appellant was selected through a
proper process, in which he obtained 114.80 marks and
placed at Serial No. 6.  We are of the opinion that
the appellant is meritorious and has, in fact, been
working for a long period.
12. In view of above, the Judgment and order passed
by the High Court is set aside and the appeal is
allowed.  In the facts and circumstances of the case,
the question of law with respect to the scope of the
power of the Commissioner is kept open for being
considered in an appropriate case.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL No.7397/2016
UNION OF INDIA & ORS. APPELLANTS
VERSUS
GAJENDRA TEWARI          RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. This appeal, by special leave granted on 08 th August,
2016, is directed against an interim order dated 14 th October,
2015 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court of Judicature
at Allahabad1, Lucknow Bench. While granting leave, this Court
stayed the operation of the impugned interim order until further
orders.
2. Having regard to the facts and circumstances projected
before us, the appeal deserves to be disposed of immediately
acknowledging that this was not such a case which required
grant of leave upon condonation of delay of 184 days on the
first  day  the  special  leave  petition  was  moved;  in  our
considered view, a notice to the respondent followed by a short
order finally disposing of the lis would have sufficed. 
3. In fact, we are pained to observe that pendency of the
1  High Court
1

--- Page 176 ---
appeal for more than a decade has had the effect of frustrating
the object and purpose of compassionate appointment, which
the respondent claimed through the writ petition 2 filed by him
before the High Court. 
4. The facts in a nutshell are these. Father of the respondent
was a postal employee who was dismissed from service on the
ground of proved misconduct by an ex parte  order dated 25 th
March, 1994. His wife preferred a departmental appeal, which
succeeded in part. The appellate order dated 21 st March, 1996
required a de novo enquiry while keeping the order of dismissal
in abeyance. Meanwhile, the father of the respondent had been
missing since 27 th  October, 1992. An FIR dated 07 th February,
1993  was  lodged.  He,  however,  remained  untraceable.
Ultimately, on 09th January, 2004, his civil death was declared
by a civil judge.
5. Respondent had applied for compassionate appointment
on 31st October, 1997 and was also offered appointment by an
order dated 05 th January, 2010. Despite the willingness of the
respondent to accept the offer and join the post offered, he was
refused permission. This resulted in the writ petition before the
High Court being instituted. 
6. By the impugned interim order, the High Court directed
2  Service Bench No.1508/2015.
2

--- Page 177 ---
that the respondent ought to be allowed to work in pursuance
of the appointment letter, provided the same has not been
canceled.
7. As noticed above, because of the interim order passed on
this appeal, the impugned order remained stayed all this while.
8. Appellants raise a contention that the relevant office
memoranda governing the field of compassionate appointment,
at the relevant time when the respondent’s claim was taken up
for consideration, did not provide for offering compassionate
appointment to a former employee who was found to have
indulged in fraud and who had not been exonerated. They
further contend that the appointment letter was erroneously
issued to the respondent; therefore, the respondent can derive
no benefit therefrom and that they were well within their right
to refuse him joining.
9. Since the writ petition is pending for decision, these are
issues which should be raised before the High Court itself in the
first instance for a decision by it and not before this Court in its
appellate jurisdiction particularly when an interim order is under
assail and not a final order.
10. In view thereof as well as long pendency of the writ
petition, we dispose of this appeal with a request to the Chief
Justice of the High Court to have the writ petition posted for
3

--- Page 178 ---
final hearing and disposal before a Bench of which the Chief
Justice is the Presiding Judge or to assign the writ petition to
any other appropriate Division Bench so as to facilitate a final
decision thereon in accordance with law, as early as possible
but preferably within a period of three months from date.
11. To expedite the process of final disposal of the writ
petition, we grant the appellants a fortnight’s time from date to
place on record their counter affidavit to the writ petition; the
respondent may file his rejoinder affidavit thereto, if any, within
a week thereafter.
12. We record the assurance of both the appellants as well as
the respondent that they shall not seek any unnecessary
adjournment before the Division Bench and cooperate with the
Hon’ble Judges to bring about an early determination of the
long pending lis.
13. All contentions/objections are left open to be raised by the
parties before the Division Bench for a decision on its own
merits.
14. Till the first date of final hearing of the writ petition, the
order of stay passed by this Court shall continue. The High
Court  may,  in  its  wisdom,  consider  the  desirability  of
extending/vacating the stay on such date, if hearing of the writ
petition does not conclude.
4

--- Page 179 ---
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

1

--- Page 209 ---
was stopped by the traffic officials for committing violation
from entering ‘No Entry Zone’. The driver is said to have
relied upon Entry Permit affixed on windshield of the
abovesaid vehicle which certificate reflected that vehicle
was having permission for plying the same in the said
Zone and certificate was valid upto 31.12.2025. On
inquiry,  it  was  found  that  the  said  certificate  was
purportedly issued by DCP, Traffic Headquarter, New Delhi
was a forged and fabricated one and no such certificate
had  ever  been  issued  by  the  said  authority.  On

the abovesaid vehicle for only three days and appellant
being the owner of the said vehicle was interrogated and
it was revealed from his statement that the earlier vehicle
was being driven by another driver – Satish and he could
not provide the details of the said driver. Thus, appellant –
owner of the vehicle was arraigned as accused. Hence,
application for anticipatory bail has been rejected under
the impugned order.

--- Page 210 ---

29.05.2026 is made absolute and appellant is ordered to

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.           OF 2026
@ SLP (CRL.) NO.11906/2026
NAZIM APPELLANT
                        VERSUS
STATE NCT OF DELHI       RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant is seeking for grant of regular bail in
respect of FIR No.121/2025 registered for the offences
punishable under Sections 103(1) and 3(5) of the Bhartiya
Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
4. It is the case of the prosecution that on 10.03.2025
at about 01:00 a.m., Akash Choudhary (complainant) and
1

--- Page 214 ---
Rohit were returning after collecting diesel and a blue
Baleno car approached them and Yamin allegedly fired at
Rohit and another occupant fired at diesel can and on
being taken to hospital, Rohit passed away while being
treated. 
5. As per the records, appellant is stated to have been
arrested and on conclusion of investigation, chargesheet
has been filed.
6. Having heard the learned counsels appearing for the
parties, we notice that the prosecution has relied upon
Akash’s account of an alleged oral dying declaration. In
fact, in the counter-affidavit, the respondent has stated
that the appellant was not present at the place of the
incident and as per CDR, his location was at Ghazipur
Dairy Farm which was near the place of the incident.
However, it is contended that he was also one of the
conspirator for killing Rohit. As to the actual role played by
the appellant, if any, will have to be unearthed only after
full-fledged trial. The appellant being in custody since
10.03.2025 and chargesheet having been filed, we are of
2

--- Page 215 ---
the considered view that he is entitled for grant of regular
bail. Hence, appeal is allowed. Impugned order is set
aside. Appellant is ordered to be released on bail on such
terms and conditions as the jurisdictional Sessions Court
may deem fit to impose. However, we make it clear that in
the event of any single incident of indulging in any
criminal act by the appellant, the prosecution would be
entitled to seek for cancellation of appellant’s bail by filing
appropriate application before the jurisdictional Court.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

1. Exemption Applications are allowed.
2. The petitioners herein seek regular bail in
connection with FIR No. 110/2026 filed at PS Ganj,
District Raipur Commissionerate, Chhattisgarh, for
the offence punishable under Section 7 of the
Chhattisgarh Gambling (Prohibition) Act, 2022.
3. The chargesheet filed on 10.06.2026, included
Section 112(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita,
2023 (for short “the BNS”) as well, and had
arrayed the petitioners herein as accused nos.7, 3
and 13, respectively. 
4. The allegation relates to the involvement of
the petitioners in an organized online gambling
group with respect to cricket betting, through an
app named “3 stumps”. It is alleged that the
petitioner-accused no.7,  Shatrughan Kumar Komre
and the petitioner-accused no.13, Sunny Dewangan
worked as operators on the app as employees of
SLP (Crl.) No.17714/2026 3

--- Page 221 ---
other  co-accused;  the  petitioner-accused  no.3,
Harsh Nagdev was engaged in running the betting
panels  for  IPL  cricket  matches.  All  the
petitioners were arrested on 15.04.2026 and have
been in judicial custody for over 1 year and 5
months. 
5. We note that several co-accused against whom
similar allegations have been raised, have already
been granted bail by this Court.
6. The impugned orders have been challenged by
raising grounds such as the petitioners not being
named in the FIR, and the likelihood of delay in
completion of trial.
7. On  a  prima  facie  consideration  of  the
material on record, we are of the opinion that the
petitioners can be released on bail, subject to
such  terms  and  conditions  that  the  Judicial
Magistrate First Class, Raipur (the jurisdictional
court)  may  deem  fit  to  impose.  Ordered
accordingly. The petitioners shall cooperate with
the trial.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.        /2026
  [@ SLP [C] NO.9580/2026]
THE FISHERIES AND FISH PRODUCTS 
MANUFACTURING CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY LIMITED   Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
THE DIRECTOR OF CO-OPERATIVE AUDIT & ORS.     Respondent(s)
O R D E R
Leave granted.
The  present  appeal  has  been  filed  by  the
appellant-cooperative Society assailing the impugned
judgement passed by the High Court of Karnataka in
Writ  Appeal  No.  1436/2025(CS-SUR),  affirming  the
findings of the learned Single Judge in a writ
petition preferred by the respondent No. 4/private
respondent. Vide the writ petition, respondent No. 4
sought for a direction to respondent Nos. 1 and 2 for
considering its representation for conducting re-
audit of the appellant-society, for the Financial
Year 2012-2013. The private respondent was elected as
the president of the appellant-society during 2009-10
and 2012-13. An issue arose with respect to the funds
utilised  for  construction  of  an  ice-plant.
Accordingly, an Audit Report was prepared by the
Departmental Auditor on 22.05.2015, citing that the
erstwhile president of the appellant society had not

--- Page 229 ---
2
obtained  permission/sanction  from  the  Managing
Committee for availing overdraft facility.  The same
resulted in financial loss by misappropriation of
funds.
Based on the aforesaid Audit Report surcharge
proceedings were initiated under Section 69 of the
Karnataka Cooperative Societies Act, 1959 (for short,
‘1959 Act’). The surcharge proceedings concluded by
holding that the appellant-society was entitled to
recover a sum of Rs. 68,85,675/- from the private
respondent,  with  an  interest  of  15%  per  annum.
Against the order dated 18.10.2022, the respondent
No. 4 filed an appeal under Section 105 of the 1959
Act before the Karnataka Appellate Tribunal, which
remains pending for consideration.
Thereafter,  the  private  respondent  filed  a
representation  seeking  re-audit  of  accounts  on
28.10.2022, which was not decided.  This resulted in
filling of the subject writ petition. The learned
Single Judge allowed the same, against which the
appellant-society preferred a writ appeal that came
to  be  dismissed  by  the  learned  Division  Bench.
Aggrieved, the appellant is before this Court.
We  have  heard  the  learned  Senior  Counsel
appearing for the appellant and the learned counsel
appearing for the respondent(s).
We have also perused the impugned judgment dated

--- Page 230 ---
3
26.11.2025 passed by the High Court.
The question for consideration in the present
appeal whether the High Court was right in issuing
the Writ of mandamus when the statutory appeal under
the  1959  Act,  against  the  order  of  surcharge
proceedings was pending consideration.
As  rightly  submitted  by  the  learned  Senior
Counsel appearing for the appellant, the High Court
has conducted a roving enquiry pertaining to the
surcharge proceedings initiated in the year 2015. It
is a settled principle that what cannot be done
directly, cannot be done indirectly.
The issues raised on behalf of the private
respondent can at best be raised in the pending
statutory  appeal  before  the  Karnataka  Appellate
Tribunal.
The audit report has been given in the year 2015
by the Departmental Auditor for the Financial Years
2012-2013 and 2013-2014.
We are not in conformity with the impugned order
passed by the learned Single Judge particularly, in
reference  to  observations  made  in  paragraph  10.
Suffice  it  is  to  state,  that  the  discretion
available for invoking the powers Article 226 of the
Constitution of India, 1950 ought not to have been
exercised in the present case.
In such view of the matter, we are inclined to

--- Page 231 ---
4
set aside the impugned judgment passed by the High
Court.  Accordingly, the impugned judgement dated
26.11.2025 passed by the Division Bench of the High
Court stands set aside.
However, the impugned judgment will not come in
the  way  of  the  private  respondent  raising  all
contentions before the Karnataka Appellate Tribunal,
including  assailing  the  audit  report  dated
22.05.2015 in the pending appeal.
The appeal is allowed, accordingly.
Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.        OF 2026
[arising out of SLP (Crl.) No. 9444 OF 2026]
SHIVLAL JATAV & ANR.                      APPELLANTS
                         VERSUS
STATE OF CHHATTISGARH                      RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Reversal of acquittal by the Appellate Court is the subject
matter of challenge in a pending revision petition 1 before the High
Court of Chhattisgarh at Bilaspur.  An order dated 18 th March, 2026
passed therein is the subject matter of challenge in this appeal.
3. The first appellant is the father of the second appellant. The
former is 80 years old and has suffered incarceration for about 16
months out the term sentence of 05 years. Similarly, the latter has
been in custody for about 14 months for an equal sentence term.
4. Considering the advanced age of the first appellant, we had
granted him interim bail by our order dated 21 st August, 2026. The
said order is made absolute on the same terms. 
5. Insofar as the second appellant is concerned, at this stage, we
see no reason to grant his prayer for suspension of sentence.
6. The  appeal stands disposed of granting liberty to the
1 Criminal Revision No. 289 of 2026

--- Page 239 ---
2
appellants to actively pursue their revision before the High Court. It
is clarified that if, despite active persuasion by the appellants and
without any fault being attributable to them, the High Court is
disabled to decide the revision within six months next from date of
communication of this order, the second appellant shall be at liberty
to renew his prayer for suspension of sentence before the High
Court.
7. We clarify that if the first appellant is found not to cooperate
with the High Court in early disposal of the revision, the High Court
shall be at liberty to cancel the bail granted to the first appellant and
take him into custody.
8. The appeal is, accordingly, partly allowed on the aforesaid
terms.
9.  Pending interlocutory application(s), if any, stand disposed of.

STATE OF KERALA                             RESPONDENT
 
O R D E R 
1.   Leave granted.
2. By the impugned judgment and order dated 20 th May, 2026,
the High Court of Kerala at Ernakulam has rejected the appellant’s
second prayer for bail in anticipation of arrest.  
3. Appellant figures as an accused in FIR No. 0113 dated 26 th
February, 2026 registered with Police Station-Vengara, District-
Malappuram. It is alleged in the FIR that the appellant has
committed offences punishable under Section 288 of the Bharatiya
Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023 and Section 4(b), 5 of the Explosive
Substances Act, 1908.

--- Page 243 ---
2
4. We have heard learned counsel appearing for the appellant as
well as the respondent.
5. It is not in dispute that the appellant, in terms of an earlier
order dated 4th June, 2026, has joined investigation. 
6. In view of the facts and circumstances, we are of the opinion
that custodial interrogation of the appellant is not necessary and
that there is sufficient ground for him to be admitted to an order for
grant of bail in anticipation of arrest.
7. Accordingly, the impugned judgment and order stands set
aside.
8. It is directed that in the event of the appellant being arrested
in connection with proceedings arising out of the aforesaid FIR, he
shall be released on bail by the arresting/investigating officer/trial
court on terms and conditions to be fixed by the trial court.
9. It is made clear that in the event the appellant breaches any
of the terms and conditions imposed by it, the trial court shall be at
liberty to cancel the bail of the appellant.
10. Needless to observe, the appellant shall not, directly or
indirectly, by making inducement, threat or promise, dissuade any
person acquainted with the facts of the case from disclosing such
facts to any police officer or to the court.
11. Also, since the investigation is yet to conclude, we direct that
if the investigating officer calls upon the appellant to join the

--- Page 244 ---
3
investigation, he shall do so by attending the police station.
12. We clarify that the observations made in this order and grant
of bail will not be treated as findings on the merits of the case.
13. The appeal is allowed on the above terms.
14.  Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO(S).       OF 2026
[@ SLP (C) NO. 3498 OF 2023]
ORISSA SANDS COMPLEX                               Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
THE STATE OF ODISHA & ORS.                         Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The present Civil Appeal by way of special leave arises
out of the order dated 19.10.2022 passed by the High Court of
Orissa in Writ Petition (C) No.  27438 of 2022.
3. The appellant herein challenged two demand notices dated
26.08.2020 and 08.09.2020 before the Revisional Authority. By
its order dated 27.07.2022, the Revisional Authority, while
allowing Revision Application No. 01 of 2020 and quashing
demand  notice  dated  08.09.2020,  dismissed  the  Revision
Application No. 02 of 2020 and upheld demand notice dated
26.08.2020.  Questioning  the  legality  and  validity  of  the
dismissal  of  Revision  Application  No.  02  by  order  dated
27.07.2022, the appellant filed a Writ Petition before the High
Court.
1

--- Page 251 ---
4. By the order impugned before us, the High Court sought
clarification in respect of judgment of this Court in Common
Cause v. Union of India 1. The clarification sought pertained to
whether the aforesaid judgment was confined to only minerals
like iron ore and manganese or extended its applicability to
other  minerals  also.  The  appellant’s  counsel  inter  alia
contended that the said judgment has no application to the
instant case as the appellants dealt with minerals other than
iron ore and manganese. Considering the aforesaid contention,
it is clear that the High Court was to study the judgment and
examine its applicability to the facts and circumstances of the
case. We are rather surprised that instead of studying the
judgment, the High Court simply directed the appellant to
approach the Supreme Court to seek interpretation of the said
judgment. We do not approve of the approach adopted by the High
Court. We have no option except to set aside the order passed
by the High Court and restore the Writ Petition to its original
number. 
5. While we do not express any opinion on the merits of the
case, we direct that the High Court will examine the judgment
and its applicability to the facts and circumstances of the
case.  We also make it clear that the parties will be entitled
to raise all contentions and objections as may be available to
them in law. 
1 (2017) 9 SCC 499
2

--- Page 252 ---
6. With these directions, the Civil Appeal stands disposed
of.

     UPON hearing the counsel, the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
The impugned order passed by a Division Bench of the Calcutta
High Court notes in clear terms that the learned single Judge,
whose orders were under appeal before the Division Bench, had
recorded  therein  that  15  others  who  had  been  appointed  on
compassionate grounds were absorbed on regular basis. 
It appears that some others, who were also given compassionate
appointments, were singled out for discriminatory treatment in
terms of their services not being regularized.  
No justification was offered by the West Bengal Essential
Commodities Supply Corporation Ltd. in the appeals filed before the
Division Bench as to how a distinction had been drawn between those
15 persons, who were regularized in service after being given
compassionate appointments, despite  the absence of a policy, while
denying the same relief to others identically situated  who were
also given similar compassionate appointments , who are now before
this Court as respondents. 
Surprisingly, the Corporation now seeks to contend that there
was  no  policy  in  the  Corporation  for  making  compassionate
appointments. If that be so, justification ought to have been
offered before the Division Bench as to why the cases of those 15
persons were treated differently. However, no justification was
offered at that stage.  Even at this time, the learned counsel for
3

--- Page 257 ---
SLP(C) No. 15757/2024 etc.
the Corporation is unable to offer any valid justification. 
The orders of the Division Bench, therefore, do not warrant
any interference.
The special leave petitions are, accordingly, dismissed
Pending applications shall stand disposed of.

maintainable;  the  Tribunal  fell  in  error  in

1. Permission to file special leave petitions is granted.
2. The submission on behalf of the petitioners is that the
Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960 (for short ‘1960 Act’)
and the Rules framed thereunder constitute a complete code where
under complaints regarding financial irregularities can be made to
the Registrar and the Registrar, inter alia,  has power to call for
audit report and, thereafter, take action if required. In such
circumstances,  there  was  no  justification  to  direct  for  a
preliminary  inquiry  by  the  police  authorities.  It  has  been
submitted  that  decision  of  this  Court  in  Lalita  Kumari  vs.
Government of Uttar Pradesh & Ors .1 does not specifically deal with
those cases where there are statutory provisions to deal with
complaints regarding financial irregularities as are found in the
1960 Act. It has also been submitted that the High Court in clear
and categorical terms did not find the allegations disclosing
commission of any cognizable offence and, therefore, a direction to
the police authorities to carry out preliminary investigation is
unwarranted particularly when there are provisions under the 1960
Act to handle complaints regarding financial irregularities etc.
3. Issue notice, returnable in six weeks.
4. In the meantime, effect and operation of the impugned order
1 (2014) 2 SCC 1
2

--- Page 314 ---
dated 02.09.2026 shall remain stayed.
5. However, it is clarified that stay of the impugned order shall
not preclude the Registrar from exercising his powers under the
provisions of the 1960 Act to direct for audit, inquiry, inspection
and supervision as per the provisions of Chapter VIII of the 1960
Act.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
We have heard learned counsel appearing for the
parties. 
The only issue which survives for consideration
of this Court is with regard to the clarification
1

--- Page 331 ---
sought in respect of direction (iii) contained in
paragraph 11 of the impugned order passed by the
Division Bench of the High Court. The said paragraph
is reproduced hereunder:-
“iii. The respondent shall bear the admission
and tuition fee of school and college upto
graduation level of the son Priyansh. Parties
shall be at liberty to quantify the expenses
for education payable monthly instead of paying
by actual expenditure each time upon production
of receipts.”
Learned counsel appearing for the petitioner
submits that it may be clarified that all educational
expenses of the son shall be borne by the respondent-
Father upto the graduation level.
Learned counsel appearing for the respondent,
on instructions, submits that the respondent shall
bear  all  educational  expenses,  including  expenses
towards transportation to and from school, uniform,
books, stationery and all other incidental expenses as
may be levied by the institution. The amount towards
such expenses may be communicated by the petitioner to
the respondent and the amount shall be paid within a
week thereof.
Another issue raised by the learned counsel
appearing for the petitioner is with regard to the
caste certificate issued in favour of the son, which
mentions the income of the father, whereas the son is
presently residing only with the mother. The marriage
2

--- Page 332 ---
between the parties has been dissolved by a decree
passed by the Family Court, which has been affirmed by
the High Court. It is, therefore, submitted that this
aspect may be incorporated in the caste certificate so
that  the  child  is  not  deprived  of  any  benefits
admissible to him on account of financial status.
Having considered the submissions so advanced,
we grant liberty to the petitioner to approach the
competent authority issuing the caste certificate for
making the necessary incorporation so that the son may
not be deprived of the appropriate status on account
of the father’s economic status. Along with the said
application, the petitioner shall submit the certified
copy  of  this  order,  whereupon  the  concerned
authorities shall pass appropriate orders.
The Special Leave Petition stands disposed of
in the aforesaid terms.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

The present appeal is a statutory criminal
appeal under Section 19 of the Terrorist and
Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987 (for
short, ’TADA’).  
The appellant has been convicted for the
offences punishable under Section 25(1A) of the
Arms Act, 1959 read with Section 120-B of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860 by the Special (TADA)
Court  and  was  sentenced  to  undergo  rigorous
imprisonment for a period of 5 years, along with
fine and default stipulations. Aggrieved by the
same, the appellant is before this Court. 
The  appellant  has  already  undergone
incarceration for a period of more than four
years and three months, out of the five years of
sentence imposed upon him. This Court was pleased
to suspend the sentence of similarly placed co-
accused persons on earlier occasions. 
In such view of the matter, we are inclined
2

--- Page 359 ---
to suspend the sentence imposed on the appellant
and grant him bail, during the pendency of the
present appeal.
Accordingly, the sentence imposed upon the
appellant stands suspended, and he is granted
bail during the pendency of the present appeal,
subject to the terms and conditions that may be
imposed by the concerned Trial Court.
The applications stand allowed.

GANGAWWA & ORS.                                    Petitioner(s)

PARVATI & ORS.                                     Respondent(s)

         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE VIJAY BISHNOI
For Petitioner(s)  Mr. Chandrashekhar A. Chakalabbi, Adv.
                   Mr. S.k Pandey, Adv.

                   Mr. Rajan Parmar, Adv.
                   Mr. Rahul Singh Latwal, Adv.
                   M/s Dharmaprabhas Law Associates- 2718, AOR
                   
                   
For Respondent(s) 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The submission on behalf of the petitioners is
that the suit instituted by the plaintiff-respondent
was for injunction and declaration with no relief
sought  for  possession.  The  trial  court  while
dismissing the suit returned a specific finding that
defendant is in possession. The First Appellate
Court allowed the appeal and without there being
1

--- Page 507 ---
even a prayer for possession, decreed the suit for
possession. The Second Appellate Court affirmed the
decree of the First Appellate Court. It has been
submitted that in absence of there being any relief
for  possession,  the  suit  for  injunction  and
declaration was not maintainable in view of the bar
of Section 34 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 and
since the finding returned by the trial court that
the defendant was in possession has not been over-
turned, the decree passed by the First Appellate
Court affirmed by the Second Appellate Court is bad
in law.
2. Delay condoned.
3. Issue notice, returnable in six weeks.
4. In the meantime, effect and operation of the
impugned decree shall remain stayed.
